passage:
The question of what it means to translate a literary work has occupied theorists since at least the Renaissance, but the terms of the debate have shifted considerably in the past half-century. An older hermeneutic tradition, broadly associated with figures like Friedrich Schleiermacher, distinguished between foreignizing translation—which preserves the alien texture of the source—and domesticating translation, which assimilates the original into the idioms and conventions of the target culture. For much of the twentieth century, this distinction operated as a normative hierarchy: the foreignizing mode was theorized as philosophically serious, an act of epistemic humility before the irreducible otherness of the source, while domestication was dismissed as a form of cultural imperialism dressed up as readability. The translator who smoothed away difficulty was accused of performing a kind of violence—not physical, but hermeneutic—on the original.

But if a commitment to foreignization were all that animated the best translators, their work would possess only the austere virtue of difficulty for its own sake. The more compelling truth is that the most accomplished translations resist both poles. Consider the anagogic dimension of translation that theorists like Henri Meschonnic have proposed: the claim that a translation participates in what Meschonnic called the poem's "rhythm," by which he meant not mere prosodic pattern but the whole movement of subjectivity as it unfolds through language. Under this view, the binary of foreignizing versus domesticating dissolves, because both poles are, in their different ways, fixated on the lexical surface—on words as portable containers of meaning—rather than on the living tissue of utterance. The translator who slavishly reproduces syntactic strangeness and the translator who substitutes fluent target-language idioms are, despite appearances, making the same mistake: both treat the source as a static object to be either preserved or replaced, rather than as a rhythmic event to be re-enacted.

This rhythmic account of translation has its detractors. Some critics argue that Meschonnic's notion of rhythm is too metaphysically freighted to bear the practical weight placed on it: how does a working translator operationalize "the movement of subjectivity"? Others, drawing on ekphrastic theory, suggest that any translation is already a form of ekphrasis—a description of one artwork in the medium of another—and that the appropriate standard is therefore not fidelity to rhythm but rather creative adequacy, a standard familiar from the translation of visual experience into verbal form. Still others, schooled in reader-response criticism, insist that the target readership's horizon of expectations matters more than any property of the source text. Each of these objections captures something real, yet each also, on inspection, reduces translation to a subspecies of some adjacent practice—paraphrase, ekphrasis, reader-response interpretation—rather than confronting it as a distinctive mode of meaning-making with its own obligations. The productive tension among these positions, rather than any single resolution, may be what best characterizes the current state of translation theory.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The foreignizing approach to translation is philosophically superior to domestication and has been consistently embraced by the most accomplished translators.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meschonnic's rhythmic theory of translation, despite its metaphysical obscurity, provides the only viable framework for evaluating literary translations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The traditional binary between foreignizing and domesticating translation has been complicated by rhythmic and other alternative theories, none of which fully resolves the debate, leaving translation as a distinctively contested practice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recent objections to Meschonnic's theory of rhythm demonstrate that translation is best understood as a subspecies of ekphrasis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The history of translation theory reveals that practical translators have always found theoretical frameworks unhelpful for their day-to-day work.

explanations.correct: The passage traces a movement from the older foreignizing/domesticating binary (paragraph 1) through Meschonnic's rhythmic alternative that dissolves that binary (paragraph 2) to a set of competing objections none of which fully prevails (paragraph 3), closing with the claim that productive tension characterizes the field. C integrates all three moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly complicates the privileging of foreignization rather than affirming it; paragraph 2 treats the binary itself as a mistake.
explanations.B: The passage presents Meschonnic's theory as compelling but then devotes an entire paragraph to serious objections; the word 'only' makes this too strong and reverses the passage's conclusion.
explanations.D: The ekphrastic objection is one of several, and the passage says it 'reduces translation to a subspecies' of adjacent practice—a criticism, not an endorsement.
explanations.E: The passage never addresses the attitudes of working translators toward theory; this is outside the passage's scope.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the competing objections to Meschonnic's rhythmic theory can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive of their philosophical pretensions but conceding their practical utility

choices.label: B
choices.text: admiring of their precision while doubting that any single one adequately accounts for translation as a distinctive practice

choices.label: C
choices.text: wholly skeptical, treating each objection as a misunderstanding of Meschonnic's core claims

choices.label: D
choices.text: enthusiastic about the ekphrastic objection in particular, regarding it as the most promising alternative

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautiously approving, suggesting that the reader-response objection ultimately supersedes the others

explanations.correct: The passage says 'Each of these objections captures something real' (acknowledging partial merit) but then adds 'yet each also, on inspection, reduces translation to a subspecies of some adjacent practice'—meaning none fully accounts for translation's distinctiveness. B precisely captures this balanced stance.
explanations.A: The passage does not characterize the objections as lacking philosophical standing; it grants them partial validity without distinguishing practical from philosophical merit.
explanations.C: The author explicitly says each objection 'captures something real,' which is the opposite of wholesale skepticism.
explanations.D: The ekphrastic objection is listed alongside two others with no signal that it is privileged; the author applies the same limiting criticism to all three.
explanations.E: No hierarchy among the three objections is established; the reader-response objection is not elevated above the others.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A theoretical binary is introduced and endorsed; a rival theory is presented and then refuted on practical grounds; the binary is reinstated as the superior framework.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An established normative hierarchy in translation theory is introduced; a more complex alternative framework is proposed as superseding that hierarchy; and several objections to that alternative are assessed, with the conclusion that no single approach resolves the debate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical survey of translation practice is offered; a contemporary practitioner's methodology is described; and the survey is used to validate the methodology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing theories are shown to be equivalent; a third theory is introduced as a synthesis; and the synthesis is demonstrated through a close reading of a specific translation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A philosophical distinction is described; a representative theorist's objection to it is summarized; and the passage concludes by calling for empirical research to settle the dispute.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents the foreignizing/domesticating hierarchy as the established norm. Paragraph 2 introduces Meschonnic's rhythmic framework as an alternative that dissolves the binary. Paragraph 3 surveys objections to that alternative and concludes that productive tension, not resolution, characterizes the field. B accurately tracks all three moves at the correct grain.
explanations.A: The binary is never reinstated; the passage moves beyond it and ends with unresolved tension rather than the binary's triumph.
explanations.C: No historical survey of actual translation practice appears, and no specific translator's methodology is validated.
explanations.D: No close reading of a specific translation appears; the synthesis (rhythm) is proposed but not demonstrated through a text.
explanations.E: The passage does not call for empirical research; it characterizes the current theoretical state as productively unresolved.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the foreignizing approach to translation was theorized by an older hermeneutic tradition as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a method for substituting fluent target-language idioms in place of the source text's syntactic structures

choices.label: B
choices.text: an act of epistemic humility before the irreducible otherness of the source text

choices.label: C
choices.text: a creative re-enactment of the source text's rhythm rather than its lexical surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: a form of cultural imperialism that disguised itself as philosophical seriousness

choices.label: E
choices.text: the preferred mode of reader-response critics who prioritized the target readership's expectations

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the foreignizing mode 'was theorized as philosophically serious, an act of epistemic humility before the irreducible otherness of the source.' B is a close paraphrase of this sentence.
explanations.A: Substituting fluent target-language idioms describes domestication, not foreignization—a direct reversal.
explanations.C: The rhythmic re-enactment concept belongs to Meschonnic's alternative framework, introduced in paragraph 2, not to the older hermeneutic tradition.
explanations.D: Cultural imperialism is how the passage characterizes the charge against domestication, not how foreignization was described.
explanations.E: Reader-response criticism is introduced in paragraph 3 as a separate, later framework; it is not associated with the older tradition's account of foreignization.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, in the author's view, both the foreignizing translator and the domesticating translator share which of the following characteristics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They give undue weight to the target readership's horizon of expectations at the expense of the source text.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They treat the source text as a static object defined by its lexical surface rather than as a dynamic event to be re-enacted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They rely on ekphrastic theory as their primary standard for evaluating creative adequacy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They reject Schleiermacher's hermeneutic framework while implicitly endorsing Meschonnic's rhythmic account.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are principally concerned with preserving the prosodic patterns of the source text rather than its semantic content.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that both the translator who 'slavishly reproduces syntactic strangeness' (foreignizing) and the translator who 'substitutes fluent target-language idioms' (domesticating) 'treat the source as a static object to be either preserved or replaced, rather than as a rhythmic event to be re-enacted.' B is a precise inference from this claim.
explanations.A: Giving weight to the target readership's expectations is the reader-response position, not a charge leveled at either the foreignizing or domesticating translators.
explanations.C: Ekphrastic theory is introduced as a distinct objection in paragraph 3 and is not attributed to either type of translator.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim that either type of translator endorses Meschonnic; the endorsement of Meschonnic is the author's own position as presented in paragraph 2.
explanations.E: The passage distinguishes Meschonnic's 'rhythm' from 'mere prosodic pattern'; neither translation type is specifically accused of fixating on prosody.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to "words as portable containers of meaning" (second paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the way in which domesticating translators misuse the vocabulary of the target language

choices.label: B
choices.text: characterize the assumption about language that, under Meschonnic's view, both foreignizing and domesticating translators share and that his theory rejects

choices.label: C
choices.text: endorse a minimalist account of translation as the faithful transfer of semantic content from one language to another

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce the concept of ekphrasis as a counterpoint to the rhythmic account of translation

choices.label: E
choices.text: summarize the reader-response argument that a text's meaning is determined by its audience rather than its author

explanations.correct: The phrase 'words as portable containers of meaning' appears in the sentence explaining why both foreignizing and domesticating translators fall short under Meschonnic's framework: both are 'fixated on the lexical surface' rather than on rhythmic re-enactment. The metaphor characterizes the shared mistaken assumption that Meschonnic's theory rejects.
explanations.A: The phrase applies equally to foreignizing and domesticating translators; it is not a critique specifically of how domesticators misuse target-language vocabulary.
explanations.C: The passage uses the phrase critically, not approvingly; it describes what Meschonnic argues both approaches wrongly assume.
explanations.D: Ekphrasis is not introduced until paragraph 3; this phrase is in paragraph 2 and has no connection to ekphrastic theory.
explanations.E: Reader-response criticism appears only in paragraph 3; the phrase does not gesture toward audience-centered interpretation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the objections raised against Meschonnic's rhythmic theory each reduce translation to a subspecies of some adjacent practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several influential translators have publicly stated that Meschonnic's prose is too obscure to be applied in practice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concept of "creative adequacy" drawn from ekphrastic theory has been shown to generate standards that apply uniquely to translation and cannot be derived from the analysis of verbal descriptions of visual art.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Meschonnic's own translations have been criticized by reader-response theorists as insufficiently attentive to the target readership's cultural context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reader-response criticism was developed in response to the perceived failures of New Criticism and has its own robust theoretical history independent of translation studies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some scholars have argued that foreignization and domestication are not truly opposite poles but occupy positions on a continuous spectrum.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that each competing objection 'reduces translation to a subspecies of some adjacent practice.' The ekphrastic objection is one of the three cited. If creative adequacy, drawn from ekphrastic theory, actually generates standards unique to translation that cannot be reduced to or derived from ekphrasis itself, then the ekphrastic objection would not be guilty of reducing translation to an adjacent practice—directly undermining the author's charge.
explanations.A: This supports the practical-operationalization objection to Meschonnic but does not address whether the competing theories reduce translation to adjacent practices; it is irrelevant to the specific claim targeted.
explanations.C: This is a criticism of Meschonnic's own practice, not a defense of the competing objections against the author's charge; it weakens Meschonnic, not the author's claim about the objections.
explanations.D: Establishing that reader-response theory has an independent history does not show that applying it to translation avoids reducing translation to reader-response interpretation; the independence of the adjacent field is beside the point.
explanations.E: The spectrum claim concerns the original foreignizing/domesticating binary and is tangential to whether the three objections to Meschonnic reduce translation to adjacent practices.
